title: A Thread Dump For Tasks Without Threads
summary: A look at open-source Rust, Tokio, and a contribution to lay the groundwork for better runtime observability

sections.heading: Snapshots of Prod
sections.body:
Imagine a production service running. No crashes, no panics and no backtrace. But requests are hanging and something inside is no longer progressing. Whats running? Whats suspended? Who is waiting on who?

In Java, one of the first tools you reach for when a service gets stuck is a [thread dump](https://medium.com/@manojkumar024/java-thread-dumps-overview-3de5d4c283bd).

Tokio's [task-dump work](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/runtime/dump/index.html) is an attempt to provide similar visibility into asynchronous Rust programs. The key differences to keep in mind though is that:

items: Java thread dumps describe OS/JVM threads
Tokio task dumps describe async tasks (which may share worker threads)
A task's "stack" get reconstructed when its future is polled and reaches suspension points.

sections.body: For more on futures take a look [here.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wXtngLBkK4Q)

sections.heading: Task? Thread?
sections.body: Tokio cannot simply copy Java’s approach. An async task does not permanently own a native stack the way an OS thread does. Tasks are closer to [green threads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_thread): lightweight units of execution scheduled by a runtime rather than directly by the operating system.

In Rust, async code revolves around `Futures`, which are essentially [state machines representing computations that may be suspended and resumed](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html). When a future cannot currently make progress, it returns `Poll::Pending`, preserving the state it will need when the runtime polls it again.

The native call stack for a task exists only while a Tokio worker thread is actively polling that task. Once the task yields, that call stack unwinds, while the future retains the task’s suspended state in its fields.

This creates a problem for observability: there is no permanently suspended native stack for a debugger to inspect later.

Tokio provides [experimental APIs](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/runtime/dump/index.html) that address this by observing a task while its future is being polled. Instrumented suspension points report where the task yields, allowing Tokio to reconstruct the logical paths through the future even though the task does not own a dedicated thread stack.

sections.heading: You Don't Have to Stop The World
sections.body:
On March of this year, [Russell Cohen](https://rcoh.me/), a senior software engineer at AWS opened an [issue](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/7975) on the Tokio repo which pointed out that the current implementation of task dumps relies on `backtrace::trace` which acquires a [global lock.](https://docs.rs/backtrace/0.3.76/src/backtrace/backtrace/mod.rs.html#52) 

As a general rule, you typically want to reduce the amount of shared state a lock acquires to what's necessary, espeicially if you're dealing with a global lock because operations that could otherwise take place independently end up punching your performance in the gut.

To give some clarity, Tokio isn't freezing the entire runtime before walking a stack. It isn't like a JVM stop-the-world pause. The issue is a bit more subtler in that every capture passed through this globally sync'd backtrace API turned an operation that should be local into a shared, process-wide contention. 

The goal here was to update the task dump code to rely on frame-pointer unwinding and lazy symbolization so that not only performance could be bought back, but that any further processing that would otherwise incur runtime costs could be handled as the caller pleased

sections.heading: Libunwind
sections.body: Here I'll give some implementation details on how we used a C API to create a global-lock-free stack walk
